Given that the point $A$ has coordinates $(\sqrt{6},\sqrt{2}),$ calculate the angle $\theta .$
questions.worked_solution:
We can form a triangle by creating a vertical line from $A$ to the $x$-axis.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216822/assets/432dbcd0967ba40a5f477d30c8e9b0985c8151fb2f13e54ad346cff4ac20c1c5.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the inverse tangent, we get

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})={30}^{∘}.
$$

Given that the point $A$ has coordinates $(-3\sqrt{3},9)$, calculate the angle $\theta .$
questions.worked_solution:
We can form a triangle by creating a vertical line from $A$ to the $x$-axis. Let us call ${\theta }^{′}$ the acute angle that is supplementary to $\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216822/assets/e0643cdb2d864b3af6466e24ab815dc8085e811dfdb86cdce253981a521faf82.png)

Using the tangent ratio, we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡{\theta }^{′}=\frac{9}{3\sqrt{3}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}.
$$

Finally, using the inverse tangent, we get

$$
{\theta }^{′}=\operatorname{arctan}⁡\sqrt{3}=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

Since $\theta +{\theta }^{′}=\pi ,$ then $\theta =\pi -{\theta }^{′}=\pi -\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$

questions.worked_solution:
We can form a triangle by creating a vertical line from $A$ to the $x$-axis. Let us call ${\theta }^{′}$ the acute angle that is formed with the $x$-axis such that ${\theta }^{′}+{180}^{∘}=\theta $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216822/assets/e3abf66be20a5ab3ed5d0b8812b127d6336cb88f8369937d415c8918d020e45e.png)

Using the tangent ratio, we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡{\theta }^{′}=\frac{(\frac{5}{4})}{(\frac{5}{4})}=1.
$$

Finally, using the inverse tangent, we get

$$
{\theta }^{′}=\operatorname{arctan}⁡1={45}^{∘}.
$$

Finally, using $\theta ={\theta }^{′}+{180}^{∘},$ we get $\theta ={45}^{∘}+{180}^{∘}={225}^{∘}.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **unit circle** is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin in the coordinate plane. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216822/assets/138322240b05231ce56ca195a06724da8a1c05ec4701ac1d9d49cadc9129c8c0.png)

The unit circle is an essential tool for understanding trigonometry. 

Suppose that we want to construct an angle $\theta$ in the coordinate plane. There is a standard way in which we do this.

- First, we draw the unit circle.

- Then, we represent $\theta$ as a central angle of the unit circle. The angle has its vertex at the origin, its initial side lies on the positive $x$-axis, and it rotates such that a positive angle is measured counter-clockwise.

For example, we represent the angles $\theta = 45^\circ, 135^\circ, 225^\circ,$ and $315^\circ$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216822/assets/1d4419633933ba2b5874873f625ca9016d42c2dc9a685c9db3619daf8512fde5.png)
